text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Junior Finance Minister Thomas Ostros does not think telecoms group Ericsson will move its headquarters abroad as the business climate is "exceptionally good" in Sweden. Ericsson chief executive Lars Ramqvist has said the company is looking into a possible move, mainly for tax reasons.
- Medical technology company Gambro, held by investment company Incentive, will become the second largest player in dialysis care in the U.S. after acquiring U.S. group Vivra for 11.5 billion crowns.

- Incentive become the second largest player in the world of dialysis care through a multi-billion crown purchase of Vivra's dialysis clinic chain. "In one year we have decreased our net debt by 10 billion crowns...and are ready to go on the offensive again," says Incentive managing director Mikael Lilius.
- The world's stockmarkets have recovered since the turbulence which started around the Easter holiday. But the Stockholm Stock Exchange is lagging behind.

- Telecoms group Ericsson pays its engineers more poorly than the national average in Sweden, the engineers union says. A salary increase would mean just as much as a tax break, according to the union.

- A billion crown affair again -- this time, Swedish investment company Incentive has bought U.S. dialysis company Vivra for 12.5 billion crowns. Just one year ago Incentive bought Gambro for 10.5 billion crowns. Health care thereby becomes the dominating business operation within the Incentive group.
- The Swedish crown continues to weaken. Since October 1996 the crown has lost 19 percent of its value against the dollar.
- The OM Group, a futures and derivatives trader, won its largest order ever -- for the first electricity bourse in the United States.
- Swedish bicycle group Monark Stiga will buy F.I.V. Edoardo Bianchi, Italy's oldest and most prestigious bicycle maker.
- The current debate about the business climate in Sweden could scare away foreign investors, says the head of Invest in Sweden, an agency to encourage foreign investment in Sweden.
